name: Damascus Steel (Wootz/Crucible Steel)
summary: High-carbon crucible steel with distinctive watered pattern, produced by smelting techniques in India and forged in the Middle East, achieving cutting performance and flexibility unmatched by European metallurgy for over a millennium.

claims.statement: Wootz steel ingots produced in southern India were traded to Damascus and Central Asia where they were forged into blades with carbon nanotube structures not reproduced until modern materials science
The production technique required precise temperature control and specific ore compositions, representing advanced empirical metallurgy without formal chemistry
The technique was lost by approximately 1750 CE and has only been partially reconstructed by modern metallurgists

evidence.source: Reibold et al. (2006) Carbon nanotubes in an ancient Damascus sabre, Nature 444
Srinivasan & Ranganathan (2004) India's Legendary Wootz Steel, National Institute of Advanced Studies
Verhoeven, Pendray & Dauksch (1998) The Key Role of Impurities in Ancient Damascus Steel Blades, JOM 50(9)
Verhoeven & Pendray (1992) Experiments to Reproduce the Pattern of Damascus Steel Blades, Materials Characterization 29(1)
Juleff (1996) An Ancient Wind-Powered Iron Smelting Technology in Sri Lanka, Nature 379

notes: Creates a new resolved cross-link: damascus_steel → precision_engineering → industrial_mass_production. Evidence quality is exceptionally high (Nature papers). Low ethical alignment reflects primary military application, but the metallurgical knowledge underpins all modern steelmaking.
